**“11/22/63” – a quick guide** --- ## 1. The book (by Stephen King) | Element | Details | |---------|---------| | **Genre** | Time‑travel thriller / historical fiction (with a strong literary‑fiction feel) | | **Publication** | 2011 (hardcover), later adapted into a 2016 Hulu miniseries | | **Premise** | A modern‑day high‑school teacher discovers a portal that leads back to 1958. He is tasked with preventing the assassination of President John F. Kennedy on November 22, 1963. | | **Main protagonist** | **Jake Epping** (aka “George” while in the past) – a 30‑something English teacher from Lisbon, Maine, who becomes an amateur historian, farmer, and, eventually, a reluctant assassin‑preventer. | | **Key supporting characters** | • **Al Templeton** – the owner of the diner that houses the time‑gate; his dying wish is to stop the JFK murder.
• **Sadie Dunhill** – a smart‑alecky, independent‑spirited librarian who falls in love with Jake.
• **Lee Harvey Oswald** – the real‑life assassin, portrayed with a mix of historical fact and King’s fictional embellishments.
• **Bill Turcotte** – a fellow “time‑traveler” who warns Jake about the dangers of altering history. | | **Plot outline (no‑spoiler version)** | 1. **Discovery** – Jake learns of the portal in a small Maine diner.
2. **Mission** – He vows to stop the assassination, believing it will create a better world.
3. **Immersion** – Jake adopts the identity “George” and lives through the late‑50s/early‑60s, learning the era’s culture, politics, and daily life.
4. **Complications** – He falls in love, makes friends, and discovers that the past resists change (the “butterfly effect”).
5. **Climax** – The fateful day arrives; Jake must decide how far he’ll go to alter history.
6. **Aftermath** – The novel explores the consequences of his actions, both personal and global, and asks whether any one person can truly rewrite the past. | | **Themes** | • **The cost of nostalgia** – the allure of a “simpler” past vs. its hidden darkness.
• **Free will vs. determinism** – how much of history is fixed?
• **The ripple effect** – small changes can explode into massive, unforeseen outcomes.
• **Love and sacrifice** – personal relationships tested by impossible circumstances.
• **The nature of heroism** – what does it mean to “save” a world? | | **Style** | King writes with his trademark blend of vivid, character‑driven storytelling and meticulous period detail. The narrative alternates between present‑day “research” chapters (with footnotes, newspaper clippings, etc.) and the immersive, first‑person account of Jake’s life in the past. | | **Reception** | Widely praised for its ambitious premise, historical accuracy, and emotional depth. It won the 2012 **British Fantasy Award** for Best Novel and was a bestseller on both sides of the Atlantic. | | **Adaptation** | Hulu’s 8‑part miniseries (2016) starring James Franco as Jake, with a strong visual recreation of 1960s America. It condenses the novel but retains the core emotional arc. | --- ## 2. The real‑world date – **November 22, 1963** | Fact | Explanation | |------|-------------| | **Event** | Assassination of **President John F. Kennedy** in Dallas, Texas. | | **Location** | Dealey Plaza, while riding in an open‑top convertible (the “Lincoln Continental”) with First Lady **Jacqueline Kennedy**, Texas Governor **John Connally**, and his wife **Nellie**. | | **Time** | 12:30 p.m. Central Standard Time (≈18:30 UTC). | | **Assassin** | **Lee Harvey Oswald**, who fired from the sixth floor of the Texas School Book Depository. He was arrested ~70 minutes later. | | **Aftermath** | Vice President **Lyndon B. Johnson** was sworn in aboard Air Force One within hours. The nation entered a period of profound mourning and political upheaval. | | **Historical impact** | • Sparked numerous conspiracy theories and investigations (Warren Commission, House Select Committee on Assassinations).
• Marked a cultural turning point—often cited as the “end of the post‑war optimism.”
• Influenced art, literature, film, and public trust in government for decades. | | **Cultural memory** | The date is instantly recognizable in the U.S. and worldwide; it appears in songs (“November 22, 1963” by The Strokes), movies, TV shows, and, of course, Stephen King’s novel. | --- ## 3. Why the two are linked - **King’s premise** hinges on the idea that if someone could travel back and stop the assassination, the entire course of modern history would change. The novel uses the **real date** as an anchor, weaving factual details (the motorcade route, the crowd’s reactions, the exact timing) into a fictional “what‑if” scenario. - The title **“11/22/63”** is simply the American date format for **November 22, 1963**, making the historical event instantly recognizable while also serving as a cryptic code for the time‑travel mission. --- ### TL;DR - **“11/22/63”** is Stephen King’s 2011 time‑travel thriller about a teacher who goes back to the late‑1950s to stop the assassination of **President John F. Kennedy** on **November 22, 1963**. - The novel blends meticulous period research, a love story, and philosophical questions about altering history. - The date itself marks the real, world‑shaking event of Kennedy’s murder—a moment that reshaped American politics and culture, and which continues to fascinate writers and audiences alike.
